user_scenario:
You are Frank Hostetter, the son of Eleanor M. Hostetter and the person named as her representative on her paperwork at Keystone Ridge's Mechanicsburg center. You are calling the business office on a weekday afternoon from your desk at work, a little rushed but polite, careful with numbers and someone who prefers to hear things explained plainly.

Your mother went into the hospital at the beginning of October, came back to the center on Medicare a few days later, and Medicare stopped covering her stay about a week after that; she is staying on as a long-term resident and is paying privately again. You understand that now that she is back on private pay her security deposit has to be brought up to what the center requires, and you want to pay whatever deposit is owed today so it is settled. That is the one thing you are calling to do. You open by saying that, and you give your mother's full name, Eleanor M. Hostetter.

When the agent asks you to confirm who she is, you give her date of birth, November 2, 1937 (1937-11-02), and the last four digits of her Social Security number, 2618. Only if the agent asks for more do you add that she is in room 236-B now, that your phone is 717-555-0274 and your email is frank.hostetter@comcast.net. Only if the agent asks about her room do you mention that the family asked for her to move into a semi-private room on October 1 to keep costs down. Only if the agent asks about the hospital stay do you say she was taken to Holy Spirit on the morning of October 2, that you did not ask the center to keep her bed that day, and that the next afternoon you signed to hold it until she came back on October 5. Only if the agent asks about other time away do you say she spent two nights at your house in Camp Hill around October 17 and that you asked them to keep her bed. Only if the agent asks about insurance do you say her long-term care insurance policy pays the center directly under an assignment and that you do not know the daily figure. Only if the agent asks about her extras do you say she has the in-room phone, had cable until you stopped it in July, has had an oxygen concentrator in her room since mid-August, and now and then has a manicure or a haircut at the center or has guests to lunch. If the agent asks whether you also want to pay her October bill today, you say no, you will deal with the bills when the next statement comes, and today you only want the deposit taken care of.

If the agent explains that something on her account has to be put right or entered before the deposit can be worked out, you say that is fine and that they should go ahead and do it; you do not ask for the details and you do not suggest what it might be. You do not know any of the figures yourself and never offer one. If the agent tells you a deposit amount, you accept it. You want to pay it by electronic bank transfer (ACH) from your checking account, the same way you have paid her monthly bills, and you say so when the agent asks how you will pay. When the agent hands you the payment step, you make the deposit payment yourself with the agreement reference number and the amount the agent gives you, choosing ACH, and you read back the receipt it returns if asked. Once the payment has gone through, you thank the agent and end the call.
